page.text_excerpt: Goose Docs Tutorial Reference Spec Library Samples Benchmarks GitHub The Goose Programming Language Why Goose Features Install a release Build and run Documentation Status License Authors History & Use of AI The Goose Programming Language A memory-safe systems language with no heap allocator, garbage collector, or lifetime annotations. In this repository's benchmarks, Goose runs faster than C++ and Rust while using less memory. Tutorial · Reference · Specification · Packages · Samples · Benchmarks · Standard library Goose has syntax familiar to C and Rust programmers, but there is no heap. Every dynamic value lives inline on a data stack managed by the compiler. Growth advances a pointer, and memory is freed when its scope ends. The language's type and lifetime rules make this memory model safe to use. Why Goose Faster than C++ and than safe Rust, while memory safe. Over sixteen benchmarks Goose runs at 3.3x the speed of idiomatic C++, 1.16x hand-optimized C++ and 1.12x the best safe Rust, on 1.9x, 1.3x and 1.2x less memory (results). These gains come from Goose's data layouts and memory model. No allocator, no GC, no reference counting, no destructors. Memory is a handful of data stacks that the compiler assigns statically. Freeing a million-element structure is one store, however deeply it nests. Growth preserves references. A reference into a growing array stays valid for as long as the array does. You keep typed references where C++ must reserve and safe Rust uses u32 indices in the corresponding benchmarks. Memory safe with zero annotations. No lifetime syntax, no aliasing or exclusivity rules, no unsafe. The compiler infers what every reference is rooted in and rejects references that could outlive their owners. Nested data stays inline. A string, an array of strings, a record with variable-size fields and an array of those records are each one contiguous block with no pointer in it. page.title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
page.description: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic technique that delivers electrical pulses to specific areas of the brain via an implant to modulate neural activity. It is already widely used for movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, and researchers are increasingly exploring its potential for severe psychiatric illnesses including major depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. However, most existing DBS systems operate in what engineers call an “open loop” manner: stimulation is delivered according to predefined settings rather than continuously adapting to the patient’s brain activity. page.text_excerpt: Some Random Thoughts.. Just a place to put some random thoughts.. Home Archive About RSS Asking LLM for confidence Amrut Joshi, October 20, 2026 LLM-based agents can do a lot of tasks. Or, at least, they can appear to do them. For example, they write code, summarize papers, plan trips, and fill in forms. If you ask one for a probability or a confidence score, it will give you one of those too. I have seen many agent designers use LLMs to generate confidence scores in this way. The problem is that there is no good reason to trust that number. This post is about why we cannot rely on an LLM to generate a confidence score. What confidence means Before we can understand why an LLM cannot give a trustworthy confidence score, we need to understand what confidence really means. For example, think of a weather forecaster who says “I am 70% confident that it’s going to rain tomorrow.” The forecaster is predicting that it will rain. The 70% is how sure they are about that prediction. Tomorrow, it will either rain or it will not, and how sure they are today depends on what they know. Their confidence comes from the information that they use. Some of it is about tomorrow: air pressure, humidity, wind, and the clouds on the radar. Some of it is from the past: years of weather records, and how often it rained after days that looked like this one. The more information they have, and the more strongly it points one way, the closer their confidence can get to 100% or to 0%. In theory, turning this information into a confidence is a calculation, not an opinion. Let’s say that this calculation can be represented by a hypothetical rule. You start with what the past tells you, and you update it with the information about tomorrow. If two forecasters have exactly the same information, and both apply the rule correctly, they must arrive at exactly the same confidence. page.text_excerpt: karpathy Home Blog Digital hygiene 17 Mar, 2025 Every now and then I get reminded about the vast fraud apparatus of the internet, re-invigorating my pursuit of basic digital hygiene around privacy/security of day to day computing. The sketchiness starts with major tech companies who are incentivized to build comprehensive profiles of you, to monetize it directly for advertising, or sell it off to professional data broker companies who further enrich, de-anonymize, cross-reference and resell it further. Inevitable and regular data breaches eventually runoff and collect your information into dark web archives, feeding into a whole underground spammer / scammer industry of hacks, phishing, ransomware, credit card fraud, identity theft, etc. This guide is a collection of the most basic digital hygiene tips, starting with the most basic to a bit more niche. Password manager. Your passwords are your "first factor", i.e. "something you know". Do not be a noob and mint new, unique, hard passwords for every website or service that you sign up with. Combine this with a browser extension to create and Autofill them super fast. For example, I use and like 1Password. This prevents your passwords from 1) being easy to guess or crack, and 2) leaking one single time, and opening doors to many other services. In return, we now have a central location for all your 1st factors (passwords), so we must make sure to secure it thoroughly, which brings us to... Hardware security key.
